content: Pelvic organ prolapse occurs when one or more pelvic organs, such as the uterus, vaginal apex, bladder, or bowel, descend into the vaginal canal. In recent years, surgeons have increasingly utilized graft materials, which can be either synthetic or biological, in transvaginal repairs. The goal of using these grafts is to reduce the recurrence of prolapse and improve outcomes compared to traditional native tissue repair, also known as colporrhaphy. This review updates the evidence on this topic, with the previous version published in 2016. The objective of this review was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of transvaginal mesh or biological grafts compared to native tissue repair or other grafts in the surgical treatment of vaginal prolapse. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared different types of vaginal repair, including mesh, biological grafts, and native tissue repair. The primary outcomes assessed were patient awareness of prolapse, the need for repeat surgery, and recurrent prolapse as determined by clinical examination. A total of 51 RCTs involving 7,846 women were included in the analysis. The certainty of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate. Transvaginal permanent mesh versus native tissue repair: Women who underwent permanent mesh repair were less likely to be aware of prolapse at six months to seven years post-surgery compared to those who had native tissue repair (risk ratio [RR] 0.83, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.73 to 0.95). This suggests that if 23% of women are aware of prolapse after native tissue repair, the rate would decrease to between 17% and 22% with mesh repair. The rate of repeat surgery for prolapse was lower in the mesh group (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.95). However, the combined rate of repeat surgery for prolapse, stress urinary incontinence, or mesh exposure was higher in the mesh group (RR 1.56, 95% CI 1.07 to 2.26). This indicates that if 7.1% of women require repeat surgery after native tissue repair, the rate would increase to between 7.6% and 16% with mesh repair. Mesh exposure occurred in 11.8% of women, and 6.1% required surgery to address mesh exposure. Recurrent prolapse on examination was less likely after mesh repair (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.55), but the certainty of this evidence was very low. Women in the mesh group had higher rates of new-onset (de novo) stress urinary incontinence (RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.88) and bladder injury (RR 3.67, 95% CI 1.63 to 8.28). There was no significant difference between the groups in rates of new-onset dyspareunia (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.79) or quality of life outcomes, although the data showed substantial variability. Transvaginal absorbable mesh versus native tissue repair: There was no significant difference between absorbable mesh and native tissue repair in terms of awareness of prolapse (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.44), repeat surgery for prolapse (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.09 to 2.40), or recurrent prolapse on examination (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.70). However, these findings were based on limited data from a single study with a small sample size. The effects of absorbable mesh on bladder-related outcomes, dyspareunia, and quality of life were uncertain due to insufficient evidence. Transvaginal biological graft versus native tissue repair: There was no significant difference between biological grafts and native tissue repair in terms of awareness of prolapse (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.56), repeat surgery for prolapse (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.77), or recurrent prolapse on examination (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.29). The certainty of the evidence ranged from low to moderate. There was no significant difference between the groups in rates of dyspareunia or quality of life outcomes. Transvaginal permanent mesh versus other permanent mesh or biological grafts: Sparse reporting of primary outcomes in these comparisons limited the ability to draw meaningful conclusions. Authors' conclusions: Permanent transvaginal mesh is associated with lower rates of prolapse awareness, repeat surgery for prolapse, and recurrent prolapse on examination compared to native tissue repair. However, it is also associated with higher rates of total repeat surgery (including for prolapse, stress urinary incontinence, or mesh exposure), bladder injury, and new-onset stress urinary incontinence. The findings from this review are consistent with the 2016 version, but the certainty and precision of the evidence have improved due to the inclusion of a larger sample size and longer follow-up data (3 to 10 years in 10 trials). The risk-benefit profile of permanent transvaginal mesh suggests it has limited utility in primary surgeries for prolapse. Its use should be carefully regulated and conducted under the oversight of local ethics committees in compliance with regulatory guidelines. Data on absorbable meshes and biological grafts do not support their use for managing transvaginal prolapse. Evidence on the management of recurrent prolapse remains of limited quality.
